markdown.headingText: Using Scrapy to Recommend a Movie from Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse
markdown.markdown:
In this section, the objective will be to create a system to recommend movies based on the amount of common actors present in other movies. Since a part of the appeal to movies are the actors playing characters within the movie and the people making the movie, one way to consider forming movie recommendations is through the frequency of these people recurring in other movies. 

Below, we will design a system that consults the website ``http://themoviedb.org`` and collects information through their movie listings and crew page. From there, the data will be adjusted and visualized to help curate a list of movies to recommend from Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse.

This topic will focus mainly on using **Scrapy** for collecting web data. Although, the section will utilize tools such as **Pandas** and **Plotly** to construct DataFrames and visualize the recommendations respectively. The package list is included in the next block.

## parse() Function Description

The `parse()` function is the first line of links this Spider takes. This function assumes that it is on the movie's home page on `http://themoviedb.org`. It will construct the URL to the "Full Cast & Crew" section, then navigate into that page. Once navigating to the next page, `parse()` will pass off to the next function, `parse_full_credits()`.

```python
    def parse(self, response):
        """
        The parse() function assumes the beginning website is the movie's site.
        This function passes to parse_full_credits() to navigate to the full
        crew and actor list. 
        """
        # Constructing url
        url_start = "http://themoviedb.org"
        url_end = response.css("p.new_button").css("a").attrib["href"]
        # Navigating to the next page. 
        yield scrapy.Request(url_start + url_end, callback=self.parse_full_credits)
```

## parse_full_credits() Function Description

The `parse_full_credits()` function involves the second line of links necessary for the given task. This function assumes it is on the movie's "Full Cast & Crew" list, which has access to a series of links to every actor and crew member's Movie Database page. The function collects all the links of the members' career pages and establishes them for the last function, `parse_actor_page()`.

```python
    def parse_full_credits(self, response):
        """
        The parse_full_credits() function assumes the website it is fed is 
        the movie's full actor and crew list. This function collects all links
        to the actors and passes to parse_actor_page(). 
        """
        # Extracting necessary links. 
        url_start = "http://themoviedb.org"
        actor_filter = response.css("ol.people.credits:not(.crew)")
        links = [url_start + r.attrib["href"] for r in actor_filter.css("div.info a")]
        
        # Visit new link and call to parse_actor_page to navigate.
        for link in links:
            yield scrapy.Request(link, callback=self.parse_actor_page)
```

## parse_actor_page() Function Description

The `parse_actor_page()` function is the last line of links necessary to collect the necessary information. This function assumes it is on an individual actor's page, where it has access to a person's complete acting history. The function collects all the links, accesses each actor's page, and collects the name and movie list of the actor. The name and movie list is stored onto a dictionary using the `yield` method. In combination with Scrapy in the terminal, the dictionary will be stored onto a `.csv` file. This file will be used for data manipulation and visualization to create the recommendation.

```python
    def parse_actor_page(self, response):
        """
        The parse_actor_page() assumes the website it is fed is an individual
        actor's website. This function collects information regarding the actor
        and every movie they participated in, then writes the collected 
        information to a csv file using the terminal in Scrapy. 
        """
        # Pulling name of actors from the website.
        actor = response.css("h2.title").css("a::text").get()
            
        for movie in response.css("a.tooltip"):
            # Pulling name of show or movie from website.
            movie_or_TV_name = movie.css("bdi::text").get()
            # Plug info into DataFrame.
            yield {
                "actor" : actor,
                "movie_or_TV_name" : movie_or_TV_name
            }
```

## Manipulating and Visualizing Scraped Data

The following blocks of code will show the process of taking the collected data and placing it in a usable form for  plotting tools. The first step involves reading the file and storing it. 

In order to count the amount of actors present in a given movie, it will start with creating a dictionary of key-value pairs, with the name of a movie and the amount of times it shows up in the above DataFrame. If the movie has been found before, it will be tracked in a list, which helps with counting the amount of appearances a movie has. This data will be sorted from a dictionary, then re-converted into a DataFrame of movies and appearance frequencies.

Lastly, we still need to visualize the data! Now that it is in a DataFrame, it will be easier to accomplish with Plotly. Using a bar graph, we can visualize the frequency of actors being present in a given movie. Specifically, we will visualize the top 10 without the source movie. 

## Recommendation & Conclusion

Thus, based off the above visualizations, if you were interested in Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, you may want to consider watching Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, Saturday Night Live, or Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-verse (when this comes out). 

Based off the work above, we are able to collect data off a website through the site's HTML and CSS formatting to use for other visualizations or applications. The process breaks down into reading through HTML and finding where the data you need is stored, writing a Spider based on this search, then storing the data in a way that can be manipulated (i.e. a CSV file).
